Title: Convert Between d, r, and Odds Ratio — d_to_r • effectsize
# Convert Between *d*, *r*, and Odds Ratio. Enables a conversion between different indices of effect size, such as standardized difference (Cohen's d), (point-biserial) correlation r or (log) odds ratios. d_to_r(d, n1, n2, ...) d_to_r(d n1 n2...) r_to_d(r, n1, n2, ...) r_to_d(r n1 n2...) oddsratio_to_d(OR, p0, log = FALSE, ...) oddsratio_to_d(OR p0 = FALSE...) logoddsratio_to_d(logOR, p0, log = TRUE, ...) logoddsratio_to_d(logOR p0 = TRUE...) d_to_oddsratio(d, log = FALSE, ...) d_to_oddsratio(d = FALSE...) d_to_logoddsratio(d, log = TRUE, ...) d_to_logoddsratio(d = TRUE...) oddsratio_to_r(OR, p0, n1, n2, log = FALSE, ...) oddsratio_to_r(OR p0 n1 n2 = FALSE...) logoddsratio_to_r(logOR, p0, n1, n2, log = TRUE, ...) logoddsratio_to_r(logOR p0 n1 n2 = TRUE...) r_to_oddsratio(r, n1, n2, log = FALSE, ...) r_to_oddsratio(r n1 n2 = FALSE...) r_to_logoddsratio(r, n1, n2, log = TRUE, ...) r_to_logoddsratio(r n1 n2 = TRUE...). ## Arguments. :   Standardized difference value (Cohen's d), correlation coefficient (r), Odds ratio, or logged Odds ratio. If either is missing, groups are assumed to be of equal size. :   Arguments passed to or from other methods. If not specified, the *d* to *OR* conversion uses am approximation (see details). :   Take in or output the log of the ratio (such as in logistic models), e.g. when the desired input or output are log odds ratios instead odds ratios. Conversions between *d* and *OR* is done through these formulae:. * \(d = \frac{\log(OR)\times\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\). * \(log(OR) = d \* \frac{\pi}{\sqrt(3)}\). Converting between *d* and *r* is done through these formulae:. * \(d = \frac{\sqrt{h} \* r}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}}\). * \(r = \frac{d}{\sqrt{d^2 + h}}\). When groups are of equal size, *h* reduces to approximately 4. The resulting *r* is also called the binomial effect size display (BESD; Rosenthal et al., 1982). If the firm uses metrics which encourage R,D&E to base program choice on anticipated market outcomes, then the impacts of risk aversion and short-termism are enormous.

results.title: Information asymmetry, risk aversion and R&D subsidies: effect-size heterogeneity and policy conundrums
results.content:
Title: Information asymmetry, risk aversion and R&D subsidies: effect-size heterogeneity and policy conundrums
# Information asymmetry, risk aversion and R&D subsidies: effect-size heterogeneity and policy conundrums. Drawing on the theory of contracts and Schumpeterian models of innovation, we demonstrate that information asymmetry and risk aversion are conducive to effect-size heterogeneity and sub-optimal allocation of R&D subsidies. Our findings reveal a policy conundrum: the case for R&D subsidies is stronger during economic downturns, when R&D investment is in basic research and when firm age, size and R&D intensity reflect success in converting R&D investment into innovative product lines; but the subsidy is less likely to increase business R&D under these conditions. results.title: The baseline of your R&D Tax Credit claim | Finerva
results.content: # The baseline of your R&D Tax Credit claim. The baseline helps companies to prove that they are producing something new and innovative. There are many existing nuances which are difficult to navigate when applying to R&D Tax Credits. ### What is the baseline? Whilst it’s difficult to define the baseline, based on HMRC’s R&D tax relief conditions%20What%20is%20the%20baseline,the%20commercial%20output%20or%20outcome.), the baseline in R&D activity is *‘the baseline in technology that any advance sought is being measured against’*. This means that the advance you are seeking is beneficial to the whole industry to be considered R&D work. The baseline is the key when claiming R&D Tax Credits as it helps companies to prove that they are producing something new and innovative. The good news is that most of the Founders have done that already – competitors & industry analysis are involved in decision-making before investing money in R&D work. However, R&D Tax Credit claims are complex.
